philanthropy

/fih-LAN-thruh-pee/ - the stress falls on LAN · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Philanthropy means organized generosity toward humanity — giving money, time, or effort on a large scale to improve other people's lives.

The aquarium owes its new research wing to local philanthropy: three families quietly covered what years of ticket sales never could.

Example

Late in life, the steel magnate turned to philanthropy with the same ferocity he had brought to business, spending his fortune down on 2,500 public libraries and declaring it a disgrace to die rich.

The scale and the aim are what make this philanthropy rather than a good deed: organized wealth pointed at the public's long-term good — literacy for strangers he would never meet. Greek phil- ('loving') plus anthropos ('human being') says it plainly: love of humankind, with a checkbook.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

charity: Charity means help given directly to those in need — a meal, a coat, a donation; philanthropy works at longer range, funding libraries, cures, and scholarships meant to fix causes rather than symptoms.

benevolence: Benevolence means the disposition to wish others well; benevolence can stay a feeling, while philanthropy is benevolence with a budget — the wish turned into funded action.

generosity: Generosity means openhandedness of any kind, to anyone — picking up a check, forgiving a debt; philanthropy aims that openhandedness at the public good, usually through causes and institutions.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

miserliness: clutching every dollar that could do good

self-interest: acting only for your own benefit

Where it sits · how large and organized the giving becomes

kindness → generosity → philanthropy

kindness vs. philanthropy: Kindness is the smallest coin of the three: one door held, one gentle word — far short of philanthropy, which builds the hospital the gentle word is spoken in.

generosity vs. philanthropy: Generosity is broader than kindness but still stops short of philanthropy: a generous person picks up the check, while a philanthropist endows the culinary school.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — phil-: loving (Greek philein, 'to love')

Root — anthrop-: human being (Greek anthropos)

Suffix — -y: state or quality of

Put it together: Phil- ('loving') plus anthropos ('human being') plus -y assembles 'the condition of loving humankind' — and the money followed the feeling, so the word now names the giving itself. Both pieces work all over English: phil- in philosophy and bibliophile, anthropos wherever human beings are the subject.

Use the root in a new word: anthropology: She switched her major to anthropology after one summer cataloging pottery shards in a dig house.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / civic

Philanthropy is the boardroom-and-broadsheet word for giving: it implies scale, organization, and a public aim, and it often names the whole sector — 'a career in philanthropy.' For one warm act, kindness or generosity fits better; for direct relief of need, charity. The person is a philanthropist; the adjective (which you may meet on test day) is philanthropic.
